turns.prompt: A coding assistant told me there was no free trial for Model X in my editor. The announcement says, “Model X is free in CodeDesk for the next three days through an API gateway.” How could it not be free?
turns.response:
The mismatch usually comes down to a technical distinction between the editor's local authentication state and how the API gateway route handles authorization checks.
Here is why your coding assistant claims it isn't free, along with how to bypass or fix the block:
Local Account Sync Delay: The editor extension checks your local account profile or active tier license key. If your account hasn't refreshed its token or doesn't explicitly have the promotional flag attached to your user ID, the UI blocks access locally before even hitting the gateway.
Gateway Route vs. Direct Key Requirement: The announcement specifies access is free "through an API gateway." If your assistant or extension is configured to use a direct provider API key (or a default paid subscription slot) instead of routing through the promotional gateway endpoint, it will enforce standard billing checks.
Model Routing Fallback: Coding assistants often default to checking local quotas. If the promotion requires selecting a specific gateway profile, dropdown preset, or proxy endpoint rather than just toggling the model name, the assistant will see a missing active subscription and flag it as unavailable.
How to Fix It
1 Force Refresh Account Auth Local sync
Open your editor settings, sign out of your account extension profile, and sign back in to force it to pull down the latest promotional entitlements.
Verification: Check your account management panel in the sidebar to ensure your current tier or promotional tag is actively displayed.
2 Verify the Gateway Endpoint Configuration Extension settings
Open your coding assistant settings and verify whether you are required to select a specific gateway URL, proxy, or promotional provider profile rather than your personal API key.
Verification: Test a prompt to see if the error changes from a billing block to a connection response.

trials.title: Godot game at a Unity meetup

turns.prompt: I made a small game in Godot. Can you playtest a Godot game at a Unity user group meetup?
turns.response:
Yes, absolutely. You can (and usually will) be welcomed to playtest a Godot game at a Unity user group meetup, but there are a few practical community dynamics to keep in mind.
Game developers are generally enthusiastic about games first and technology second. However, because user groups are organized around specific ecosystems, knowing what to expect can help you get the best feedback.
How the Meetup Will View Your Game
The "Engine Refugee" Factor: A massive wave of developers migrated from Unity to Godot. Many attendees at a Unity meetup are likely familiar with Godot, have tried it, or are actively using it for side projects. You won't be as much of an oddity as you might think.
Game First, Engine Second: When you hand someone a controller or a keyboard to playtest, they care about whether the game is fun, how the controls feel, and if there are bugs—not whether it was compiled with C# scripts in Unity or GDScript in Godot.
Friendly Engine Ribbing: Expect some light-hearted jokes or friendly banter (e. g., “Oh nice, look at you not paying runtime fees” or someone joking about Godot's node hierarchy). Take it in stride; it's all part of gamedev culture.
Tips for a Successful Playtest
Check the Vibe First: Some local chapters are strictly tailored technical workshops (e. g., deep-diving into a specific Unity DOTS package or URP shader). If it's a structured technical lecture, save your game for the social/networking hour afterward. If it's an open " indie showcase, " "project night, " or "coworking" meetup, pitch it right away.
Bring a Portable Build: Make sure your game runs effortlessly on your laptop or can be quickly pulled up via an HTML5/web export if they want to try it in a browser. Don't waste valuable meetup time trying to troubleshoot export templates or missing dependencies.
Focus on Feedback: Phrase your request around design: "I'd love to get eyes on the difficulty curve" or "Can you see if this jump feels responsive?" rather than engine architecture, unless you happen to run into another Godot developer in the room who wants to talk code.
If you want a more targeted technical critique on things like Godot's scene tree or performance profiling, look up if your city has a local Godot Meetup or an engine-agnostic group like an IGDA (International Game Developers Association) chapter or a general indie arcade night.
 Otherwise, your local Unity group will likely be happy to check out what you built!

That is definitely a hotter take! The 1982 Poltergeist is usually revered as a foundational classic of 1980s horror and blockbuster filmmaking, so finding it "insanely terrible" puts you in a pretty bold camp.
When people bounce off the original today, it usually comes down to a few specific things:
Pacing and Tone: It takes its time building up the suburban family dynamic, leaning heavily into 80s Amblin-style wonder and comedy before any real horror kicks in. For modern viewers used to relentless, fast-paced terror, the first hour can feel a bit sluggish.
Aged Practical Effects: While groundbreaking in 1982, stop-motion skeletons, rubber faces, and classic optical compositing can look a bit quaint or campy compared to seamless modern CGI.
The Director Debate: A lot of cinephiles argue that Steven Spielberg's heavy creative footprint (he co-wrote, produced, and reportedly directed large chunks of it alongside Tobe Hooper) results in a sanitized, PG-13 "horror for kids" vibe that lacks genuine, teeth-gritting dread.

turns.prompt: I want to do something in New York City this weekend. Pick three options that cost less than $25 per person and tell me what each one costs. The budget is firm.
turns.response:
Here are three great options to experience New York City this weekend, all strictly under your $25-per-person budget limit:
1. Staten Island Ferry & Harbor Views
What it is: Take a round-trip ride on the iconic yellow commuter ferry connecting Whitehall Terminal in Lower Manhattan to St. George in Staten Island. It provides a stunning, close-up look at New York Harbor, the Statue of Liberty, and the Lower Manhattan skyline.
You can easily grab a drink or snack onboard and enjoy the views from the outdoor deck.
Cost: $0.00 (Completely free)
2. Central Park Zoo
What it is: Located right in the heart of Manhattan, this compact and historic zoo features snow leopards, red pandas, sea lions, and a dedicated Tisch Children’s Zoo. It is an ideal, manageable weekend afternoon activity that lets you experience wildlife without breaking the bank.
Cost: $22.95 per person for the Total Experience Package (includes the main zoo, children's zoo, and 4-D theater).
3. Self-Guided Architectural & High Line Walk
What it is: Spend your afternoon strolling along the High Line—an elevated, linear public park built on a historic freight rail line above Manhattan’s West Side—and transition into exploring the unique modern architecture and public art installations of the adjacent Hudson Yards and Chelsea neighborhoods.
Cost: $0.00 (Free admission; completely self-guided)
